proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(P\in\mathrm{Base}_\kappa\) and \(t\in\{0,1\}\).  Define the finite Borel measure
\[
 \mu_{t,P}(C):=P^{\mathrm{obs}}\{X\in C,T=t\},\qquad C\in\mathcal B(D).
\]
By sharp assignment, \(\mathbf 1\{T=t\}=\mathbf 1\{X\in A_t\}\) almost surely.  In particular, for every Borel set \(C\subseteq A_t\), consistency, sharp assignment, the tower property, and the definition of \(m_{t,P}\) give, successively,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \int_C g_{t,P}(z)\,\mu_{t,P}(dz)
 &=E_{P^{\mathrm{obs}}}\!\left[Y\mathbf 1\{X\in C,T=t\}\right] \\
 &=E_P\!\left[Y(t)\mathbf 1\{X\in C,T=t\}\right] \\
 &=E_P\!\left[E_P\{Y(t)\mid X\}\mathbf 1\{X\in C,T=t\}\right] \\
 &=\int_C m_{t,P}(z)\,\mu_{t,P}(dz).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the indicator \(\mathbf 1\{X\in C,T=t\}\) is \(\sigma(X)\)-measurable because sharp assignment makes \(T\) a measurable function of \(X\).  The displayed identity for all such \(C\) proves
\[
 g_{t,P}=m_{t,P}\quad \mu_{t,P}\text{-almost everywhere on }A_t.
\tag{1}
\]
Thus \(m_{t,P}|_{A_t}\) is a version of the observed conditional regression on the restricted support.  This step uses no unconfoundedness premise: within \(A_t\), treatment is already fixed by \(X\).

Let \(E_{t,P}\subseteq A_t\) be a measurable set of full \(\mu_{t,P}\)-measure on which (1) holds.  For \(x\in B\) and \(0<h\le h_0\), sharp assignment and the definition of the side masses imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mu_{t,P}\bigl(B_2(x,h)\bigr)
 &=P\{X\in B_2(x,h),T=t\} \\
 &=P\{X\in B_2(x,h)\cap A_t\} \\
 &=q_t(x,h).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(P\in\mathrm{Base}_\kappa\), the base-mass assumption, \(c_m>0\), and \(h>0\) yield
\[
 \mu_{t,P}\bigl(B_2(x,h)\bigr)=q_t(x,h)\ge c_m h^\kappa>0.
\tag{2}
\]
Consequently \(x\) belongs to the closure of the support of \(\mu_{t,P}\).  More precisely, because \(\mu_{t,P}(A_t\setminus E_{t,P})=0\), (2) gives
\[
 \mu_{t,P}\bigl(E_{t,P}\cap B_2(x,h)\bigr)>0
\tag{3}
\]
for every admissible \(h\).  With \(h_j=h_0/(j+1)\), choose \(z_j\in E_{t,P}\cap B_2(x,h_j)\), which is possible by (3).  Then \(z_j\to x\), and every \(z_j\) lies in the closed \(h_0\)-neighborhood of \(B\).  The causal-mean Lipschitz assumption and (1) therefore imply
\[
 \left|g_{t,P}(z_j)-m_{t,P}(x)\right|
 =\left|m_{t,P}(z_j)-m_{t,P}(x)\right|
 \le L\lVert z_j-x\rVert_2
 \le Lh_j\longrightarrow0.
\tag{4}
\]
By the definition \(\theta_{t,P}=m_{t,P}|_B\), equation (4) identifies the side trace as \(\theta_{t,P}(x)=m_{t,P}(x)\).

The value in (4) is independent of conditional-expectation versions.  Indeed, suppose \(v\) and \(w\) are two Lipschitz representatives on the relevant side that represent the same observed regression class.  Their equality set has full \(\mu_{t,P}\)-measure, so (3), applied to that equality set, supplies \(z_j\to x\) with \(v(z_j)=w(z_j)\).  Continuity then gives
\[
 |v(x)-w(x)|
 \le |v(x)-v(z_j)|+|w(z_j)-w(x)|
 \le 2L\lVert z_j-x\rVert_2\longrightarrow0.
\tag{5}
\]
Thus the observed regression equivalence class has exactly one Lipschitz extension value at each \(x\in B\).  Equivalently, if the conditional mean in the statement is represented by the smooth version \(m_{t,P}|_{A_t}\), then Lipschitz continuity directly yields the ordinary side limit
\[
 \lim_{\substack{z\to x\\ z\in A_t}}
 E_{P^{\mathrm{obs}}}[Y\mid X=z,T=t]
 =\lim_{\substack{z\to x\\ z\in A_t}}m_{t,P}(z)
 =m_{t,P}(x)=\theta_{t,P}(x),
\tag{6}
\]
and (4)--(5) show that (6) is an observed-law functional rather than an artifact of the selected version.

For completeness, let \(P\) and \(P'\) be two members of \(\mathrm{Base}_\kappa\) having the same observed law.  They then have the same measure \(\mu_t\) and the same observed conditional-regression equivalence class.  Applying (3)--(5) to the two Lipschitz versions \(m_{t,P}|_{A_t}\) and \(m_{t,P'}|_{A_t}\) gives
\[
 m_{t,P}(x)=m_{t,P'}(x),\qquad x\in B,\quad t\in\{0,1\}.
\tag{7}
\]
Hence each \(\theta_{t,P}\) is identified by \(P^{\mathrm{obs}}\).  Finally, by the definitions of the two boundary traces and of the causal contrast,
\[
 \tau_P(x)=\theta_{1,P}(x)-\theta_{0,P}(x)
 =m_{1,P}(x)-m_{0,P}(x),\qquad x\in B,
\]
so \(\tau_P\) is identified on \(B\), as claimed.

Put \(A=\bar\kappa-2\).  By the exponent-window assumption,
\[
 \epsilon\leq \alpha=\kappa-2\leq A.
\]
We first verify the two score laws.  Direct Cartesian integration gives
\[
 \int_D \frac{\alpha+1}{4}|r|^\alpha\,dr\,ds
 =\frac{\alpha+1}{4}\frac{2}{\alpha+1}\,2=1.
\]
The number \(V_{\mathrm{disk}}\) is the Lebesgue area of the unit disk, by its
vertical-slice definition.  For \(0\leq \rho\leq1\), the identity
\(1-\rho^\alpha=\int_\rho^1\alpha t^{\alpha-1}\,dt\), nonnegative integration,
and the linear scaling of area yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
 4-Z_\alpha
 &=\int_{\{z:\|z\|_2\leq1\}}(1-\|z\|_2^\alpha)\,dz\\
 &=\int_0^1\alpha t^{\alpha-1}
       \operatorname{Leb}\{z:\|z\|_2\leq t\}\,dt\\
 &=V_{\mathrm{disk}}\int_0^1\alpha t^{\alpha+1}\,dt
 =V_{\mathrm{disk}}\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the asserted formula for \(Z_\alpha\) is exact.  Moreover, the integrand
defining \(Z_\alpha\) is at most one, while on
\(\{(r,s)\in D:|r|\geq1/2\}\), a set of area two, it is at least
\(2^{-\alpha}\).  Consequently
\[
 2^{1-\alpha}\leq Z_\alpha\leq4.
 \tag{1}
\]
Both displayed densities are therefore nonnegative Borel functions of integral
one.  Each is positive away respectively from the line \(r=0\) or the single
point \((0,0)\); every nonempty relatively open subset of \(D\) contains a
positive-Lebesgue-measure subset on which the corresponding density is positive.
Hence both score laws have support \(D\).

Fix \(x=(0,s_0)\in B\) and \(0<h\leq h_0\).  Since
\(|s_0|\leq1/2\) and \(h_0\leq1/8\), the entire Euclidean ball of radius \(h\)
about \(x\) lies in \(D\), and every point in that ball has norm at most
\(|s_0|+h\leq5/8\).  Reflection in the line \(r=0\) shows that the two
one-sided masses agree for either score density; the convention at \(r=0\) is
irrelevant because both laws are absolutely continuous.

For the pervasive density, vertical Cartesian slices give, for either
\(t\in\{0,1\}\),
\[
 q_t^{\mathrm{perv}}(x,h)
 =\frac{\alpha+1}{2}\int_0^h r^\alpha\sqrt{h^2-r^2}\,dr
 =C_\alpha h^{\alpha+2}=C_\alpha h^\kappa.
 \tag{2}
\]
The half-ball contains the rectangle with
\(0\leq |r|\leq h/2\) on the relevant side and
\(|s-s_0|\leq h/2\).  It is contained in the rectangle with
\(0\leq |r|\leq h\) and \(|s-s_0|\leq h\).  Integrating the pervasive density
over these rectangles gives
\[
 \frac{\alpha+1}{4}h\int_0^{h/2}r^\alpha\,dr
 =2^{-\alpha-3}h^\kappa
 \leq q_t^{\mathrm{perv}}(x,h)
 \leq \frac{\alpha+1}{4}(2h)\int_0^h r^\alpha\,dr
 =\frac12h^\kappa.
 \tag{3}
\]
These rectangles remain inside \(D\) at both endpoints of \(B\).

For the isolated density, consider on the relevant side the rectangle
\(h/2\leq |r|\leq3h/4\), \(|s-s_0|\leq h/4\).  Its area is \(h^2/8\), it lies
in the radius-\(h\) ball because \((3/4)^2+(1/4)^2<1\), and its points have
norm at least \(h/2\).  Using \(Z_\alpha\leq4\) from (1),
\[
 q_t^{\mathrm{iso}}(x,h)
 \geq \frac1{Z_\alpha}\frac{h^2}{8}\left(\frac h2\right)^\alpha
 \geq2^{-\alpha-5}h^\kappa.
 \tag{4}
\]
Conversely, the relevant half-ball is contained in a rectangle of area
\(2h^2\), and throughout that rectangle intersected with the ball its norm is
at most \(|s_0|+h\).  The lower bound on \(Z_\alpha\) in (1) therefore gives
\[
 q_t^{\mathrm{iso}}(x,h)
 \leq 2^{\alpha-1}\,2h^2(|s_0|+h)^\alpha
 =2^\alpha h^2(|s_0|+h)^\alpha.
 \tag{5}
\]
If \(|s_0|\geq2h\), use instead the rectangle
\(0\leq|r|\leq h/2\), \(|s-s_0|\leq h/2\), of area \(h^2/2\).  On it,
\(\|z\|_2\geq |s_0|-h/2\geq |s_0|/2\).  Again using
\(Z_\alpha\leq4\),
\[
 q_t^{\mathrm{iso}}(x,h)
 \geq\frac14\frac{h^2}{2}left(\frac{|s_0|}{2}\right)^\alpha
 =2^{-\alpha-3}h^2|s_0|^\alpha.
 \tag{6}
\]

At the origin the clipping in the density is inactive on the ball.  The
preceding nonnegative-integral calculation on the unit disk also gives
\[
 \int_{\{\|z\|_2\leq1\}}\|z\|_2^\alpha\,dz
 =V_{\mathrm{disk}}-V_{\mathrm{disk}}\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+2}
 =\frac{2V_{\mathrm{disk}}}{\alpha+2}.
\]
Linear scaling by \(h\) and reflection across \(r=0\) now imply
\[
 q_t^{\mathrm{iso}}(0,h)
 =\frac{V_{\mathrm{disk}}}{(\alpha+2)Z_\alpha}h^{\alpha+2}
 =D_\alpha h^\kappa.
 \tag{7}
\]

We next verify the class constants.  Since \(\alpha\leq A\), (3)--(4) imply
for both score laws
\[
 q_t(x,h)\geq 2^{-A-5}h^\kappa=c_mh^\kappa.
 \tag{8}
\]
For the pervasive law, (3) and
\(C_m=2^A+1>1/2\) show that every site of \(B\) is thin at level
\(C_mh^\kappa\).  The points
\(s_j=-1/2+jh\), \(0\leq j\leq\lfloor1/h\rfloor\), form an
\(h\)-separated subset of \([-1/2,1/2]\), while no such subset has more than
\(\lfloor1/h\rfloor+1\) points.  Hence
\[
 J_{P^{0,\mathrm{perv}}}(h,C_mh^\kappa)
 =\lfloor1/h\rfloor+1\geq h^{-1}=c_Jh^{-1}.
 \tag{9}
\]
For the isolated law, (5) at \(s_0=0\) gives
\(q_t^{\mathrm{iso}}(0,h)\leq2^\alpha h^\kappa<C_mh^\kappa\), so the origin is
a thin site for every admitted \(h\).

It remains to prove the full isolated profile rather than only its thinnest
level.  Let \(u\geq0\) and suppose
\(a_{P^{0,\mathrm{iso}}}((0,s_0),h)\leq u\).  The two side masses are equal, so
(6) shows that either \(|s_0|<2h\), or
\[
 |s_0|\leq 2\,8^{1/\alpha}left(\frac{u}{h^2}\right)^{1/\alpha}.
\]
Thus the thin set is contained in the centered interval of radius
\[
 R=2h+2\,8^{1/\alpha}left(\frac{u}{h^2}\right)^{1/\alpha}.
\]
An \(h\)-separated subset of an interval of radius \(R\) has cardinality at
most \(1+2R/h\).  Since \(\alpha\geq\epsilon\), it follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
 J_{P^{0,\mathrm{iso}}}(h,u)
 &\leq5+4\,8^{1/\alpha}h^{-1}
       \left(\frac{u}{h^2}\right)^{1/\alpha}\\
 &\leq \left(5+4\,8^{1/\epsilon}\right)
   \left\{1+h^{-1}\left(\frac{u}{h^2}\right)^{1/\alpha}\right\}.
\end{aligned}
 \tag{10}
\]
This derivation holds for every \(u\geq0\), so in particular it holds for every
required \(C_mh^\kappa\leq u\leq1\), including \(u=1\).  Equations (8)--(10),
together with the definitions of the base, isolated, and pervasive classes,
establish all score-law membership conditions with the constants in the claim.

We now construct the full-data laws.  For either score density, take the product
of its Borel probability measure with two independent standard Gaussian
measures, let \(X,Z_0,Z_1\) be the coordinate maps, and apply the Borel maps in
the Gaussian-tent definition to obtain \(T,Y(0),Y(1),Y\).  This gives a Borel
causal law and gives sharp assignment and consistency pointwise.  Write \(P^0\)
for the corresponding baseline law and \(P^{j,h}\) for its tent law at \(x_j\).
Under a baseline law, \(m_{0,P}=m_{1,P}=0\).  Under a tent law,
\[
 m_{1,P}(z)=a_{\mathrm{tent}}\psi_{j,h}(z),\qquad
 m_{0,P}(z)=-a_{\mathrm{tent}}\psi_{j,h}(z).
 \tag{11}
\]
The distance map is one-Lipschitz and the positive-part map is one-Lipschitz;
hence \(\psi_{j,h}\) is \(h^{-1}\)-Lipschitz.  Because
\(a_{\mathrm{tent}}=Lh/4\), both means in (11) are \(L/4\)-Lipschitz, and their
boundary traces have absolute value at most
\(a_{\mathrm{tent}}\leq Lh_0/4\leq L/32<L\).  Conditional on \((X,T)\), the
centered observed error is
\(\sigma\{TZ_1+(1-T)Z_0\}\), so for every \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\),
\[
 E\!\left[\exp\!\left(\lambda\sigma\{TZ_1+(1-T)Z_0\}\right)\mid X,T\right]
 =\exp(\sigma^2\lambda^2/2).
 \tag{12}
\]
Thus every baseline and tent law satisfies the smoothness, envelope, and
sub-Gaussian requirements.  Tents change no score marginal, so (8)--(10) put
each tent law in the same profile class as its baseline.  At its active center
\(x_j\), (11) gives
\[
 \|\tau_{P^{j,h}}-\tau_{P^0}\|_\infty
 \geq \tau_{P^{j,h}}(x_j)-\tau_{P^0}(x_j)
 =2a_{\mathrm{tent}}=Lh/2.
 \tag{13}
\]

For completeness, we compute the squared-tent integrals without circular
coordinates.  Let \(d(z)=\|z-x_j\|_2\) and let \(\mu_{\mathrm{perv}}\) denote
the pervasive score law.  By (2), for \(0\leq t\leq h\),
\[
 \mu_{\mathrm{perv}}\{d(X)\leq t\}=2C_\alpha t^\kappa.
\]
The elementary identity
\[
 (1-d/h)_+^2=\int_d^h\frac2h(1-t/h)\,dt
\]
(with the integral interpreted as zero when \(d>h\)) and nonnegative
integration give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \int_D\psi_{j,h}^2 f_{\mathrm{perv},\alpha}
 &=\int_0^h\frac2h(1-t/h)\,2C_\alpha t^\kappa\,dt\\
 &=\frac{4C_\alpha}{(\kappa+1)(\kappa+2)}h^\kappa
 =Q_{\mathrm{perv},\alpha}h^\kappa,
\end{aligned}
 \tag{14}
\]
because \(\kappa+1=\alpha+3\) and \(\kappa+2=\alpha+4\).  At the centered
isolated site, (7) similarly gives
\(\mu_{\mathrm{iso}}\{\|X\|_2\leq t\}=2D_\alpha t^\kappa\), and the same
calculation yields
\[
 \int_D\psi_{0,h}^2 f_{\mathrm{iso},\alpha}
 =Q_{\mathrm{iso},\alpha}h^\kappa.
 \tag{15}
\]

Finally, under a tent law the conditional observed mean relative to its baseline
is \(\mu_j(X,T)=(2T-1)a_{\mathrm{tent}}\psi_{j,h}(X)\).  Direct expansion of
the logarithm of the two equal-variance Gaussian densities gives conditional
Kullback--Leibler divergence \(\mu_j(X,T)^2/(2\sigma^2)\).  Since the score laws
are identical, (14) and \(a_{\mathrm{tent}}^2=L^2h^2/16\) imply
\[
 \operatorname{KL}(P^{j,h,\mathrm{perv}}_{\mathrm{obs}},
                    P^{0,\mathrm{perv}}_{\mathrm{obs}})
 =\frac{L^2Q_{\mathrm{perv},\alpha}}{32\sigma^2}h^{\kappa+2}.
\]
The log likelihood ratio for an independent product is the sum of its
one-observation log likelihood ratios.  Taking expectations therefore gives
\[
 \operatorname{KL}\!\left((P^{j,h,\mathrm{perv}}_{\mathrm{obs}})^{\otimes n},
 (P^{0,\mathrm{perv}}_{\mathrm{obs}})^{\otimes n}\right)
 =\frac{nL^2Q_{\mathrm{perv},\alpha}}{32\sigma^2}h^{\kappa+2}.
 \tag{16}
\]
Replacing (14) by (15) proves the centered isolated formula.

All displayed constants are uniform on the exponent window.  Indeed, (1),
(3), (4), and (7) bound \(Z_\alpha,C_\alpha,D_\alpha\) above and away from zero
using only \(\epsilon\) and \(A\); division by
\((\alpha+3)(\alpha+4)\) does the same for both \(Q\)-coefficients.  The class
constants themselves are the fixed values \(2^{-A-5}\), \(2^A+1\), \(1\), and
\(5+4\cdot8^{1/\epsilon}\).  At \(\kappa=3\), one has \(\alpha=1\) and
\[
 C_1=\int_0^1w\sqrt{1-w^2}\,dw=\frac13,
 \qquad Q_{\mathrm{perv},1}=\frac{4(1/3)}{4\cdot5}=\frac1{15}.
\]
Substitution into (16) gives exactly
\(nL^2h^5/(480\sigma^2)\), completing the proof.

proposed_definition_changes.proposed:
For \(0<h\leq h_0\) and \(u\in[0,\infty)\), set
\(J_P(h,u)=\max\{|F|:F\subseteq\{x\in B:a_P(x,h)\leq u\},
\|x-x'\|_2\geq h\text{ for distinct }x,x'\in F\}\), with value zero for an
empty thin set.
proposed_definition_changes.reason: The class definitions evaluate \(J_P(h,C_mh^\kappa)\), but the frozen signature restricts the second argument to \([0,1]\). With the common choice \(C_m=2^{\bar\kappa-2}+1\), this threshold can exceed one at the smallest exponent in the window. Extending the unchanged packing formula to every \(u\geq0\) makes all class conditions well typed and preserves every value on the original domain.

proposed_core_edits.name: JP
proposed_core_edits.reason: The second-argument type must contain \(C_mh^\kappa\) for every declared exponent and radius; the packing construction is meaningful for all nonnegative thresholds.

proofs.proof_tex:
Write \(m=n_1\) and \(\ell=\log(en)\).  The case \(m=0\) is harmless:
the restriction \(mu\geq C\ell\) is then empty, while the definitions give
\(q_t^L=0\leq q_t\leq1=q_t^U\).  We henceforth take \(m\geq1\).

For \(t\in\{0,1\}\), \(s\in[-1/2,1/2]\), and \(h\in H_n\), put
\[
 C_{t,s,h}=\{z\in A_t:\|z-(0,s)\|_2\leq h\}.
\]
On any fixed collection \(z_1,\ldots,z_N\), and for fixed \(t,h\), membership
of \(z_i=(r_i,s_i)\) in \(C_{t,s,h}\), as a function of \(s\), is the
indicator of the closed interval
\[
 \left[s_i-\sqrt{h^2-r_i^2},
       s_i+\sqrt{h^2-r_i^2}\right]
\]
when \(z_i\in A_t\) and \(|r_i|\leq h\), and is identically zero otherwise.
Consequently the trace changes only at at most \(2N\) endpoints.  The number
of traces of
\[
 \mathcal C_n=\{C_{t,s,h}:t\in\{0,1\},
 s\in[-1/2,1/2],\ h\in H_n\}
\]
on \(N\) points is therefore at most
\[
 2|H_n|(2N+1)\leq C_0(N+1)\ell.                 \tag{1}
\]

We record the relative deviation calculation, including its constants.
For a Bernoulli variable \(Z\) with mean \(p\), the inequalities
\(e^v-1-v\leq v^2/[2(1-|v|/3)]\), \(|v|<3\), and exponential Markov give
\[
 \Pr\!\left\{|\widehat p-p|>
 2\sqrt{\frac{3p\ell}{m}}+\frac{6\ell}{m}\right\}
 \leq2e^{-6\ell}                                      \tag{2}
\]
for a fixed set.  To make (2) uniform, introduce an independent sample of
size \(m\), apply (2) conditionally to the pooled \(2m\) observations, and
sum over their traces.  Equation (1) bounds the number of those traces by
\(C_0(2m+1)\ell\).  A second application of (2) to the ghost empirical
probability removes the conditioning.  Thus, after enlarging a numerical
constant only,
\[
 \Pr\!\left\{\exists C\in\mathcal C_n:
 |P(C)-\widehat P_m(C)|
 >
 \sqrt{\frac{12\widehat P_m(C)\ell}{m}}
 +\frac{20\ell}{m}\right\}\leq C_1n^{-3}.      \tag{3}
\]
For clarity, the passage from the version with \(P(C)\) in (2) to (3) is
pure algebra: if \(d=|P(C)-\widehat P_m(C)|\), then
\(\sqrt{P(C)}\leq\sqrt{\widehat P_m(C)}+\sqrt d\);
substitution in (2), followed by
\(2ab\leq a^2+b^2\), absorbs one half of \(d\) into the left side and leaves
the two displayed constants in (3).  This also proves (3) for sets whose
pooled trace occurs at a breakpoint, because closed endpoints were retained.

Let \(\mathcal E_{1n}\) be the event in (3).  Since
\(\widehat P_m(C_{t,s,h})=\widehat q_t^{(1)}((0,s),h)\), (3) and the
definition of \(b_n\) give, simultaneously in \(x,t,h\),
\[
 q_t^L(x,h)\leq q_t(x,h)\leq q_t^U(x,h),\qquad
 a^L(x,h)\leq a_P(x,h)\leq a^U(x,h).             \tag{4}
\]
If \(m q_t(x,h)\geq C_2\ell\), the same algebra, with \(C_2\) sufficiently
large, gives
\[
 \frac12q_t(x,h)\leq q_t^L(x,h)
 \leq q_t(x,h)\leq q_t^U(x,h)\leq2q_t(x,h).       \tag{5}
\]
Applying (5) to a side attaining the minimum and using (4) on the other side
gives the asserted constant-factor comparison for \(a^L,a^U,a_P\).

We next prove the packing comparison at the same physical radius.  The
sample breakpoints in \(C_1(h)\) are exactly the points at which one of the
empirical ball traces can change.  The deterministic mesh used in the
corrected construction has spacing at most \(h/16\).  Hence for every
\(x=(0,s)\in B\) there is a point \(g_h(x)\in G_1(h)\) such that
\[
 \|g_h(x)-x\|_2\leq h/16,\qquad
 \widehat q_t^{(1)}(g_h(x),h)
 =\widehat q_t^{(1)}(x,h),\quad t=0,1.            \tag{6}
\]
Indeed, at a breakpoint take the breakpoint itself; in an open cell take
its midpoint.  Refinement by the deterministic mesh makes the cell length
at most \(h/16\).  This proves (6), including closed-ball endpoint cases.

Let \(F\) be an \(h\)-separated subset of
\(\{x:a_P(x,h)\leq u\}\), and for each \(x\in F\) choose a side \(t_x\)
with \(q_{t_x}(x,h)\leq u\).  On \(\mathcal E_{1n}\), equations (3) and (6)
imply
\[
 a^U(g_h(x),h)
 \leq C_3\{u+\ell/m\}.                             \tag{7}
\]
Moreover distinct images are separated by at least \(7h/8\).  Upward dyadic
rounding multiplies a positive argument by at most two, except below the
smallest positive grid value, where the additional amount is at most
\((m\vee1)^{-1}\) and is already absorbed by \(\ell/m\).  Taking the
constant denoted by \(c\) in the statement at least \(2C_3\), (7) proves
\[
 J_P(h,u)\leq
 \widehat J\!\left(h,c\{u+\ell/m\}\right).         \tag{8}
\]
The corrected definition accepts every nonnegative second argument and caps
it at one before rounding, so (8) is also well typed at \(u=1\).

Conversely, every qualifying point \(g\) in the maximum defining
\(\widehat J(h,v)\) satisfies, by (4),
\[
 a_P(g,h)\leq a^U(g,h)\leq
 \min\{1,C_4(v+\ell/m)\}.                          \tag{9}
\]
Order any \(h/2\)-separated qualifying set along the segment and split it
into its odd and even indexed points.  Each part is \(h\)-separated.
Both parts are also \(h/8\)-separated and, by monotonicity of ball mass in
the radius, are thin at radius \(h/8\) at the level in (9).  Therefore
\[
 \widehat J\!\left(h,c\{u+\ell/m\}\right)
 \leq
 C_5J_P\!\left(h/8,C_5\{u+\ell/m\}\right).         \tag{10}
\]
Equations (8)--(10) are the claimed comparison.

All maps used above are Borel.  The square-root breakpoint is continuous on
its closed domain; inclusion of a candidate is Borel; sorting a finite
source-labeled list and retaining the least label use finitely many Borel
comparisons.  The deterministic refinement, midpoint operation, and the
maximum over subsets of a finite ordered set are likewise Borel.

For completeness, we bound the exceptional terms used by the estimator.
Apply (3) also to the independent second half.  Choose
\(h^\circ\in H_n\) with
\[
 n^{-1/(4\bar\kappa)}\leq h^\circ
 <2n^{-1/(4\bar\kappa)}.
\]
By the base-mass assumption and \(\kappa\leq\bar\kappa\),
\[
 n_2a_P(x,h^\circ)\geq
 c\,n(h^\circ)^{\bar\kappa}\geq c n^{3/4}
 \quad\text{uniformly in }x.                      \tag{11}
\]
Equations (4)--(5), the deterministic bound
\(J_P(h,u)\leq1+2/h\), and (10) show that \(h^\circ\) is admissible for every
\(x\), for all sufficiently large \(n\).  The selected criterion is no
larger than
\[
 d_n=C\left\{
 Ln^{-1/(4\bar\kappa)}
 +\sigma n^{-3/8}\sqrt{\ell}\right\}.              \tag{12}
\]
Its variance term and admissibility consequently imply
\[
 \inf_x n_2a_P(x,\widehat h(x))
 \geq c\,d_n^{-2}\geq c n^{1/(2\bar\kappa)}.       \tag{13}
\]
The second-half version of (3), or the fixed-set bound (2) followed by the
trace count (1), now gives
\[
 \Pr\{\exists x,t:N_t^{(2)}(x,\widehat h(x))=0\}
 \leq Cn^{-3}.                                     \tag{14}
\]
The same event also rules out an empty admissible-bandwidth set, by (11).
For the finitely many smaller \(n\), increase \(C\).  Thus the probability in
the theorem is at most \(C\ell^2/n\).  Projection bounds the contrast loss by
\(4L\), so the exceptional expected contribution is at most
\(C(L+\sigma)\ell^2/n\).

Finally, on \(\mathrm{Iso}_\kappa\), put
\(b=n^{-1/(\kappa+2)}\), up to a factor-two dyadic adjustment, and write
\(a_P(x,b)=wb^\kappa\).  The lower-mass assumption gives \(w\geq c_m\), and
the isolated envelope gives
\[
 J_P(b,\min\{1,Ca_P(x,b)\})
 \leq C\{1+w^{1/(\kappa-2)}\}.                    \tag{15}
\]
Since
\[
 \sup_{\substack{\kappa\in K\\w\geq c_m}}
 \frac{1+\log(e+w^{1/(\kappa-2)})}{w}<\infty,
\]
the severity-layer contribution at (15) is \(O(b)\), while the exceptional
term is \(o(b)\), uniformly on \(K\).  This is the asserted absence of a
leading global logarithm.

The corrected construction uses only finitely many Borel operations on
\(I_1\) at each \(h\in H_n\).  The preceding lemma proves measurability of
\(C_1,G_1,\widehat J,a^L,a^U\).  A minimum over the finite ordered set \(H_n\),
with the stipulated smallest-minimizer rule, is Borel.  The second-half
counts and sums are finite Borel sums, their zero-count branch is explicit,
and both projections are continuous.  Hence \(\widehat\tau_n\) is a total
Borel map.  Its formula contains neither \(\kappa\) nor a class label.

Put \(\ell=\log(en)\), and, with the numerical constant \(C_0\) supplied by
the packing comparison, define
\[
 V_P(x,h)=Lh+\sigma
 \sqrt{\frac{
 1+\log\!\left(eJ_P(h,\min\{1,C_0a_P(x,h)\})\right)}
 {na_P(x,h)}}.                                    \tag{16}
\]
The base-mass assumption makes every denominator in (16) positive.  Let
\[
 \mathcal R_P=\sup_{x\in B}\inf_{h\in H_n}V_P(x,h).
\]
On the first-half event \(\mathcal E_{1n}\) of the preceding lemma, positivity
of \(a^L(x,h)\) implies
\((n_1\vee1)a_P(x,h)\geq c\ell\); indeed
\(\widehat q_t^{(1)}>b_n(\widehat q_t^{(1)})\) on both sides, and (3) then
gives this inequality.  Thus (5), (8), and (10), applied also at the rounded
level \(\widehat u(x,h)\), show that every admissible empirical criterion
\[
 \widehat V(x,h)=Lh+4\sigma
 \sqrt{\frac{1+\log(e\widehat J(h,\widehat u(x,h)))}
 {n_2a^L(x,h)}}
\]
obeys
\[
 C_1^{-1}V_P(x,h)
 \leq\widehat V(x,h)
 \leq C_1V_P(x,h)+C_1\sigma\frac{\ell^2}{n}.       \tag{17}
\]
The additive term covers the bottom dyadic severity cell.  If an
\(h\) attaining the finite infimum in (16) is not empirically admissible,
(3) and (8) imply \(V_P(x,h)\geq c\sigma\).  In that case the projected loss
is at most \(4L\), which is bounded by \(C V_P(x,h)\), with \(C\) allowed to
depend on the fixed ratio \(L/\sigma\).  Otherwise minimization and (17) give
\[
 \widehat V(x,\widehat h(x))
 \leq C\inf_{h\in H_n}V_P(x,h)
      +C\sigma\frac{\ell^2}{n}.                   \tag{18}
\]
Thus (18) holds in the risk bound in both cases; an empty admissible set is
kept in the explicit exceptional event in the statement.

We next establish the stochastic step rather than assuming it.  Conditional
on all scores and on \(I_1\), write
\[
 \varepsilon_i
 =Y_i-T_im_{1,P}(X_i)-(1-T_i)m_{0,P}(X_i),
 \qquad i\in I_2.
\]
The conditional sub-Gaussian assumption and independence give, for every
deterministic index set \(A\subseteq I_2\),
\[
 E_P\!\left[
 \exp\!\left\{\lambda\sum_{i\in A}\varepsilon_i\right\}
 \,\middle|\,X_1,\ldots,X_n,I_1\right]
 \leq\exp\!\left(\frac{\sigma^2\lambda^2|A|}{2}\right).   \tag{19}
\]
Exponential Markov and minimization over \(\lambda\) therefore give
\[
 P\!\left\{\left|\sum_{i\in A}\varepsilon_i\right|
 >\sigma\sqrt{2|A|z}\,\middle|\,X_1,\ldots,X_n,I_1\right\}
 \leq2e^{-z}.                                      \tag{20}
\]

Here is the required flat profile peeling.  Fix a side and a bandwidth, order
the centers along \(B\), and partition them according to the dyadic cells of
their population side mass.  A maximal \(h\)-separated subset of the cell
whose upper mass is \(u\) has at most \(J_P(h,u)\) points, because
\(\{x:q_t(x,h)\leq u\}\subseteq\{x:a_P(x,h)\leq u\}\).
Every remaining center is within \(h\) of one of these points.  Within such
an interval, each score contributes to the ball sum on one interval of
centers, as displayed in the proof of (1).  Successive bisection at its
endpoints and (19) give
\[
 P\!\left[
 \sup_{\substack{x:q_t(x,h)\leq u\\
                  q_t(x,h)>u/2}}
 \frac{\left|\sum_{i\in I_2}
 \varepsilon_i\mathbf1\{X_i\in A_t,\|X_i-x\|_2\leq h\}\right|}
 {N_t^{(2)}(x,h)\vee1}
 >
 C\sigma\sqrt{\frac{1+\log(eJ_P(h,u)) +z}{n_2u}}
 \right]\leq2e^{-z}.                              \tag{21}
\]
To verify the endpoint bisection in (21), expose the at most \(2N\) interval
endpoints one at a time.  At level \(r\), at most \(2^rJ_P(h,u)\) partial
sums occur, while their unexplained conditional variance is at most
\(2^{-r}n_2u\sigma^2\).  Applying (20) with
\(z+\log(eJ_P(h,u))+2r\) and summing
\(\sum_{r\geq0}e^{-2r}\) yields (21).  The event
\(N_t^{(2)}<n_2q_t/2\) is bounded by the same calculation with centered
Bernoulli indicators and is absorbed by increasing \(C\).

Apply (21) successively at
\[
 u_j=\min\{1,2^j a_P(x,\widehat h(x))\},\qquad j=0,1,\ldots,
\]
and stop when \(u_j=1\).  The numerator in (21) grows as \(2^{j/2}\), whereas
division by the count contributes \(2^{-j}\); hence the resulting
expectations are bounded by
\[
 C\sigma\sqrt{
 \frac{1+\log\!\left(
 eJ_P(\widehat h(x),
 \min\{1,C_0a_P(x,\widehat h(x))\})\right)}
 {n_2a_P(x,\widehat h(x))}}
 \sum_{j\geq0}2^{-j/2}.                            \tag{22}
\]
There is no factor equal to the number of severity cells.  If selected
bandwidths differ, perform the same bisection after ordering the selected
intervals by decreasing radius.  An interval not contained in a previously
charged interval contributes an \(h\)-separated center to the appropriate
packing; a contained interval is charged to the next bisection level of its
ancestor.  Thus the very same geometric series in (22) controls all
\(h\in H_n\).  This is a deterministic one-dimensional charging: every
interval is charged once, and at charge depth \(r\) its variance is at most
\(2^{-r}\) times its ancestor's variance.  Integrating (21) in \(z\), using
\(\int_0^\infty e^{-z}\,dz=1\), gives
\[
 E_P\!\left[
 \sup_{\substack{x\in B,\ t\in\{0,1\}\\
 N_t^{(2)}(x,\widehat h(x))>0}}
 \left|
 \frac{\sum_{i\in I_2}\varepsilon_i
 \mathbf1\{X_i\in A_t,\|X_i-x\|_2\leq\widehat h(x)\}}
 {N_t^{(2)}(x,\widehat h(x))}
 \right|
 \,\middle|\, I_1\right]
 \leq
 C\sup_{x\in B}\{V_P(x,\widehat h(x))-L\widehat h(x)\}
 +C\sigma\frac{\ell^2}{n}.                        \tag{23}
\]
The bottom severity cell and the complement of the two relative-deviation
events contribute the last term, by (3), (19), and integration of (20).

For a positive second-half count, conditional mean Lipschitzness gives
\[
 \left|
 \frac{\sum_{i\in I_2}m_{t,P}(X_i)
 \mathbf1\{X_i\in A_t,\|X_i-x\|_2\leq h\}}
 {N_t^{(2)}(x,h)}
 -\theta_{t,P}(x)\right|\leq Lh.                  \tag{24}
\]
Because \(\theta_{t,P}(x)\in[-L,L]\), projection onto \([-L,L]\) cannot
increase the error in (24).  Projection onto \([-2L,2L]\) likewise cannot
increase contrast error.  Sum (24) over the two sides, combine (18) and
(23), and use the \(4L\) loss bound on a zero-count or empty-admissible-set
sample.  This yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
 E_P\|\widehat\tau_n-\tau_P\|_\infty
 &\leq C\mathcal R_P+C\sigma\frac{\ell^2}{n}\\
 &\quad+4L\,P\!\left\{\exists x\in B:
 \min_tN_t^{(2)}(x,\widehat h(x))=0
 \mathbin{\text{or}}
 \nexists h\in H_n,
 n_2a^L(x,h)\geq64[1+\log\{e\widehat J(h,\widehat u(x,h))\}]
 \right\}.
\end{aligned}                                      \tag{25}
\]
Equation (25) is exactly the displayed oracle inequality.  Equations
(11)--(14) in the preceding lemma bound its event probability by
\(C\ell^2/n\), uniformly over \(\kappa\in K\), completing the proof.

The construction of \(\widehat\tau_n\) contains neither \(\kappa\) nor the
names \(\mathrm{Iso}_\kappa,\mathrm{Perv}_\kappa\); thus it remains only to
evaluate the oracle inequality for the two classes.

Fix \(\kappa\in K\).  For the isolated class, let
\(b=n^{-1/(\kappa+2)}\), and choose \(h_b\in H_n\) with
\(b\leq h_b<2b\), which is possible for all sufficiently large \(n\).
Write
\[
 a_P(x,h_b)=w_xh_b^\kappa.
\]
The base-mass assumption gives \(w_x\geq c_m\).  Choose the numerical
constant in the theorem so that \(C_0c_m\geq C_m\).  The isolated envelope,
with \(\alpha=\kappa-2\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 J_P(h_b,\min\{1,C_0a_P(x,h_b)\})
 &\leq C_{\mathrm{iso}}\left\{
 1+h_b^{-1}
 \left(\frac{C_0w_xh_b^\kappa}{h_b^2}\right)^{1/\alpha}
 \right\}\\
 &\leq C\{1+w_x^{1/\alpha}\}.                     \tag{26}
\end{aligned}
\]
The same inequality holds when the threshold is clipped at one, by
monotonicity and the envelope at \(u=1\).  Since
\(\epsilon\leq\alpha\leq\bar\kappa-2\),
\[
 \sup_{\alpha\in[\epsilon,\bar\kappa-2]}
 \sup_{w\geq c_m}
 \frac{1+\log(e+Cw^{1/\alpha})}{w}<\infty.         \tag{27}
\]
Also \(nh_b^\kappa\asymp h_b^{-2}\).  Substitution of (26)--(27) into
(16) therefore yields, uniformly in \(x,P,\kappa\),
\[
 V_P(x,h_b)
 \leq CLh_b+C\sigma
 \sqrt{\frac{1+\log(e+Cw_x^{1/\alpha})}
 {nh_b^\kappa w_x}}
 \leq Cb.                                         \tag{28}
\]
The remainder \(\log^2(en)/n=o(b)\) uniformly on the compact exponent
window.  The theorem and (28) prove
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathrm{Iso}_\kappa}
 E_P\|\widehat\tau_n-\tau_P\|_\infty
 \leq Cn^{-1/(\kappa+2)}.                         \tag{29}
\]

For the pervasive endpoint, in fact for every
\(P\in\mathrm{Base}_\kappa\), every \(h\)-separated subset of the segment
\(B\) has at most \(1+1/h\leq2/h\) elements.  Hence
\[
 J_P(h,u)\leq2/h                                  \tag{30}
\]
for every \(u\geq0\).  Let
\(r=(\log n/n)^{1/(\kappa+2)}\), and choose
\(h_r\in H_n\) with \(r\leq h_r<2r\).  By base mass, (30), and
\(\log(e/h_r)\leq C\log n\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sup_{x\in B}V_P(x,h_r)
 &\leq CLh_r+
 C\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\log(e/h_r)}
 {nc_mh_r^\kappa}}\\
 &\leq C(\log n/n)^{1/(\kappa+2)}.                \tag{31}
\end{aligned}
\]
Again the theorem's remainder is of smaller order uniformly on \(K\).
Since \(\mathrm{Perv}_\kappa\subseteq\mathrm{Base}_\kappa\), (31) gives
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathrm{Perv}_\kappa}
 E_P\|\widehat\tau_n-\tau_P\|_\infty
 \leq C(\log n/n)^{1/(\kappa+2)}.                 \tag{32}
\]
The same single total estimator appears in (29) and (32), so the simultaneous
endpoint-adaptation claim follows.

proposed_definition_changes.proposed:
Split the sample into \(I_1\) and \(I_2\).  Let
\[
 H_n=\{h_02^{-j}:0\leq j\leq\lceil\log_2n\rceil\},
 \qquad
 U_n=\{0,1\}\cup
 \{2^{-\ell}:0\leq\ell\leq\lceil\log_2(n_1\vee1)\rceil\}.
\]
On \(I_1\), set
\[
 \widehat q^{(1)}_t(x,h)
 =(n_1\vee1)^{-1}\sum_{i\in I_1}
 \mathbf 1\{X_i\in A_t,\ \|X_i-x\|_2\leq h\}.
\]
With
\[
 b_n(v)=\sqrt{\frac{12v\log(en)}{n_1\vee1}}
       +\frac{20\log(en)}{n_1\vee1},
\]
set
\[
 q^U_t=\min\{1,\widehat q^{(1)}_t+b_n(\widehat q^{(1)}_t)\},
 \qquad
 q^L_t=\max\{0,\widehat q^{(1)}_t-b_n(\widehat q^{(1)}_t)\},
\]
\[
 a^U=\min_tq^U_t,\qquad a^L=\min_tq^L_t.
\]
For \(h\in H_n\), form the source-labeled list consisting of
\((-1/2,0,0)\), \((1/2,0,1)\), and every
\[
 \left(S_i+e\sqrt{h^2-R_i^2},i,e\right),
 \qquad i\in I_1,\quad e\in\{-1,1\},
\]
for which \(|R_i|\leq h\) and
\(S_i+e\sqrt{h^2-R_i^2}\in[-1/2,1/2]\).
Sort lexicographically by boundary coordinate, then by \(i\), then by \(e\),
and discard repeated coordinates after retaining the least source label.
Write the remaining coordinates as
\(-1/2=z_0<\cdots<z_M=1/2\), and define
\[
 C_1(h)=((0,z_0),\ldots,(0,z_M)).
\]
Put \(M_h=\lceil16/h\rceil\), and sort the finite union
\[
 \{z_0,\ldots,z_M\}
 \cup\{-1/2+j/M_h:0\leq j\leq M_h\}
\]
as \(-1/2=w_0<\cdots<w_Q=1/2\).  Define the refined grid
\[
 G_1(h)=\{(0,w_j):0\leq j\leq Q\}
 \cup
 \left\{\left(0,\frac{w_j+w_{j+1}}2\right):0\leq j<Q\right\}.
\]
For \(v\geq0\), let \(u(v)\) be the smallest element of \(U_n\) which is at
least \(\min\{1,v\}\), and set
\[
 \widehat J(h,v)
 =1\vee\max\left\{|F|:
 \begin{array}{l}
 F\subseteq G_1(h),\\
 \|x-x'\|_2\geq h/2\ \text{for distinct }x,x'\in F,\\
 a^U(x,h)\leq u(v)\ \text{for every }x\in F
 \end{array}\right\}.
\]
Let \(\widehat u(x,h)\) be the smallest element of \(U_n\) at least
\(\min\{1,4a^U(x,h)\}\).  On \(I_2\), set
\[
 N^{(2)}_t(x,h)=\sum_{i\in I_2}
 \mathbf1\{X_i\in A_t,\ \|X_i-x\|_2\leq h\}.
\]
Define
\[
 \widetilde Y^{(2)}_t(x,h)=0
 \quad\text{if }N^{(2)}_t(x,h)=0,
\]
and otherwise define
\[
 \widetilde Y^{(2)}_t(x,h)
 =\frac{1}{N^{(2)}_t(x,h)}
   \sum_{i\in I_2}Y_i
   \mathbf1\{X_i\in A_t,\ \|X_i-x\|_2\leq h\}.
\]
Set
\[
 \overline Y^{(2)}_t(x,h)
 =\Pi_L(\widetilde Y^{(2)}_t(x,h)).
\]
Among \(h\in H_n\) satisfying
\[
 n_2a^L(x,h)\geq
 64\{1+\log(e\widehat J(h,\widehat u(x,h)))\},
\]
choose the smallest minimizer of
\[
 Lh+4\sigma
 \sqrt{\frac{1+\log(e\widehat J(h,\widehat u(x,h)))}
 {n_2a^L(x,h)}}.
\]
Denote it by \(\widehat h(x)\), and set
\(\widehat h(x)=h_0\) if the admissible set is empty.  Finally set
\[
 \widehat\tau_n(x)=
 \Pi_{2L}\!\left(
 \overline Y^{(2)}_1(x,\widehat h(x))
 -\overline Y^{(2)}_0(x,\widehat h(x))\right).
\]
proposed_definition_changes.reason: The original breakpoint grid was built for one radius while the empirical packing predicate used a different radius, and the grid had no deterministic mesh guaranteeing a nearby trace-equivalent representative. The corrected construction refines the sample breakpoints by a deterministic mesh, evaluates empirical thickness at the same radius, and caps nonnegative packing thresholds before dyadic rounding. These changes are forced by the same-scale packing proof.

proposed_core_edits.name: JHat
proposed_core_edits.reason: The packing-comparison statement evaluates the empirical count at a constant multiple of a probability plus a confidence radius, which can exceed one. The corrected definition accepts a nonnegative input and caps it at one before rounding.
